---
title: "Least Squares — The Best Approximate Line"
description: "A compact linear-algebra lesson with mathematical definitions, real values and reasoning."
---

## Start with a question

Three measurements do not lie on one perfect line. How do we draw a line that is as close as possible to all three?

## Understand the central idea

When a system has no exact solution, choose model parameters that minimise the sum of squared residuals.

## Express it with mathematics

$$
\hat{\beta}=\arg\min_{\beta}\|X\beta-y\|_2^2
$$

**Every symbol explained:** X is the design matrix of input measurements, β is a vector of unknown model coefficients, y is the measured output vector, ||·||² is the sum of squared residuals, arg min is the parameter choice achieving the smallest value, and the hat denotes the fitted estimate.

**Substitute real numbers:** Fit a constant prediction β to observations y=(1,2,3). The squared error is (β−1)²+(β−2)²+(β−3)². At β=2 it is 1+0+1=2; at β=1 it is 0+1+4=5. Differentiating gives 6β−12=0, so β=2 is optimal.

## Why this works

For a constant predictor, minimising squared differences gives the arithmetic mean. For multiple columns, the normal equations XᵀXβ=Xᵀy arise from setting derivatives to zero.

## What can go wrong?

In numerical software, directly forming (XᵀX)^−1 can be unstable or impossible if X lacks full column rank. QR or SVD-based solvers are preferred.

## Your turn

Find the best constant for observations (2,4,9), and compute the squared error.
